variants.title: Run the parsing pipeline
variants.context: A file becomes an accepted record in five stages: ingest safely, recover page content, build structure, apply the schema contract, then accept or route the candidate. Each stage adds evidence and none may erase the original source or an earlier decision.
variants.prompt: A supplier uploads a mixed PDF bundle and the product needs an accepted record from it. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Recover page content: use native objects where trustworthy and render and OCR only the pages that need recognition.
Build structure: resolve reading order, sections, key-value pairs, tables, and cross-page continuations while keeping coordinates.
Ingest safely: verify file signatures and limits, assign a stable document ID, hash the bytes, and store them immutably.
Accept or review: release safe candidates, send bounded uncertainty to review, or quarantine an unsafe source.
Apply the contract: normalize typed values, validate required fields and relationships, and attach confidence and provenance.

variants.hint: Which stage decides whether any model is allowed to see the bytes at all?
variants.explanation: Ingestion is a security boundary that runs before recognition, and every later stage appends evidence rather than replacing what came before.

variants.prompt: A date printed as 04/05/26 has to become a normalized value a downstream system can trust. Put the handling in order.

items.text: Validate the normalized value against the schema and the document's other dates.
Record confidence, calibration cohort, and decision state with the field candidate.
Keep the raw text and the locale evidence that surrounds it.
Recover the raw characters from the page along with their coordinates.
Emit the normalized typed date alongside the raw text rather than replacing it.

variants.hint: Ask what a newer parser would need in order to replay this same field.
variants.explanation: Evidence is preserved before normalization so a correction stays inspectable and a later parser can replay the same source.

variants.title: Run the parsing pipeline
variants.context: A file becomes an accepted record in five stages: ingest safely, recover page content, build structure, apply the schema contract, then accept or route the candidate. Each stage adds evidence and none may erase the original source or an earlier decision.
variants.prompt: A new parser version is ready to ship. Put the reversible release path in order.

items.text: Promote through a canary whose exposure is capped by document family, tenant, or action.
Review evaluation results by slice together with capacity and review-load assumptions.
Keep a rollback trigger and a replay procedure for affected source IDs.
Freeze an immutable input corpus that the new parser version was not trained on.
Run the old and new versions on those same inputs and compare candidates.

variants.hint: Reversibility depends on something being kept, not on the release being cautious.
variants.explanation: Running both versions on immutable inputs is what makes a comparison meaningful and lets affected source IDs be replayed after a rollback.

variants.title: Guard the intake boundary
variants.context: Ingestion is a trust boundary because the parser processes attacker-controlled bytes. Identify the source immutably, verify the file rather than trusting its suffix, enforce budgets before fan-out, and isolate processing with least privilege and separate quarantine storage.
variants.prompt: An anonymous upload endpoint receives a PDF. Put the intake steps in order.

items.text: Verify the file: compare the allowlisted extension, declared MIME type, file signature, and parser probe.
Identify the source: assign a document ID and tenant, hash the original bytes, and preserve page order.
Isolate processing: run parsers with least privilege, restricted network and filesystem access, and separate quarantine storage.
Enforce budgets: limit bytes, pages, dimensions, attachments, decompressed size, nesting depth, and time.

variants.hint: Two files with the same name are not the same file; what settles that first?
variants.explanation: Identity is established before inspection so retries refer to the same revision, and budgets are enforced before fan-out multiplies the work.

variants.title: Guard the intake boundary
variants.context: Ingestion is a trust boundary because the parser processes attacker-controlled bytes. Identify the source immutably, verify the file rather than trusting its suffix, enforce budgets before fan-out, and isolate processing with least privilege and separate quarantine storage.
variants.prompt: A file named report.pdf is actually a zip archive that expands to 400 times its compressed size. Put the handling in order.

items.text: The decompressed-size budget trips before any parser fan-out begins.
The upload is quarantined in separate storage with the suspicious-expansion reason recorded.
The document ID is assigned and the original bytes are hashed and stored immutably.
The file signature probe disagrees with the declared PDF MIME type and the suffix.

variants.hint: The suffix is the least trustworthy thing about this file.
variants.explanation: Signature and budget checks run before parsing because the expansion is only dangerous once a library starts decompressing it.

variants.title: Guard the intake boundary
variants.context: Ingestion is a trust boundary because the parser processes attacker-controlled bytes. Identify the source immutably, verify the file rather than trusting its suffix, enforce budgets before fan-out, and isolate processing with least privilege and separate quarantine storage.
variants.prompt: Text extracted from an untrusted invoice will later be summarized by an LLM. Put the trust handling in order.

items.text: Apply the LLM's instruction-isolation rules to the text before it enters the prompt.
Carry the untrusted label with the extracted text through structure and schema stages.
Apply the escaping rules of any index, template engine, or browser that receives the same text.
Store the original bytes immutably and record the source as untrusted at intake.

variants.hint: Extraction changes the format of the bytes, not their provenance.
variants.explanation: Extracted text stays untrusted input, so the trust label travels with it and each downstream system applies its own isolation rules.

variants.title: Size the two queues
variants.context: Capacity planning uses work units, not documents. Incoming pages per minute is documents per minute times average pages per document, and review load per hour is documents per minute times 60 times the review routing rate.
variants.prompt: A pipeline receives 45 documents per minute and routes 12 percent of documents to human review. What is the review load in documents per hour?
variants.hint: Review load is driven by documents, not by pages.
variants.explanation: Review load per hour is documents per minute times 60 times the routing rate, which is what tells you whether reviewer capacity can absorb the parser's output.

mistakes.feedback: That is the hourly document arrival rate with the routing rate never applied.
That is documents per minute sent to review; the question asks per hour.

variants.title: Size the two queues
variants.context: Capacity planning uses work units, not documents. Incoming pages per minute is documents per minute times average pages per document, and review load per hour is documents per minute times 60 times the review routing rate.
variants.prompt: A tenant sends 24 documents per minute averaging 14 pages each, and the parser pool sustains 480 pages per minute. How many pages per minute of headroom remain?
variants.hint: Convert the arrival rate into work units before comparing it with capacity.
variants.explanation: Incoming pages per minute is documents per minute times average pages per document, and headroom is what absorbs bursts, retries, and slow pages.

mistakes.feedback: The 14 pages per document were never applied, so arrivals were counted as 24 pages per minute.
That is the incoming page rate itself, not the capacity left over.

variants.title: Size the two queues
variants.context: Capacity planning uses work units, not documents. Incoming pages per minute is documents per minute times average pages per document, and review load per hour is documents per minute times 60 times the review routing rate.
variants.prompt: Arrivals run at 60 documents per minute, 15 percent are routed to review, and each reviewer completes 20 documents per hour. How many reviewers does the steady-state load need?
variants.hint: Work out the hourly review load before dividing by per-reviewer throughput.
variants.explanation: A faster parser can overload the human queue, so reviewer count is derived from the routed load rather than assumed constant.

mistakes.feedback: That is the review load in documents per hour, not the number of reviewers it needs.
The 15 percent routing rate was skipped and every arriving document was sent to review.

variants.title: Place the check at its level
variants.context: Validation happens at five levels: syntactic checks types and enumerations, field checks domain rules, structural checks sections, tables, and source anchors, cross-field checks reconciliation across values, and action validation asks whether the evidence is sufficient for the specific downstream decision.
variants.prompt: A team is writing the validation plan for an extraction schema. Match each level to what it checks.

pairs.label: Syntactic validation
pairs.detail: The output parses and conforms to expected types and enumerations.

pairs.label: Field validation
pairs.detail: Identifiers, dates, currencies, units, and allowed values satisfy domain rules.

pairs.label: Structural validation
pairs.detail: Required sections, table headers, row relationships, page coverage, and source anchors exist.

pairs.label: Cross-field validation
pairs.detail: Totals reconcile, date ranges are ordered, and identifiers agree across pages.

pairs.label: Action validation
pairs.detail: The evidence is sufficient for the specific downstream decision being taken.

variants.hint: Two levels look at one value at a time and two look at how values relate.
variants.explanation: The levels are separate because a record can pass every type and domain rule and still be insufficient evidence for the action it is about to authorize.

variants.title: Place the check at its level
variants.context: Validation happens at five levels: syntactic checks types and enumerations, field checks domain rules, structural checks sections, tables, and source anchors, cross-field checks reconciliation across values, and action validation asks whether the evidence is sufficient for the specific downstream decision.
variants.prompt: Five candidates fail in different ways. Match each failure to the validation level that catches it.

pairs.label: The response is not valid JSON and one enum value is unrecognized
A currency amount uses a locale format the domain rules do not allow
A table lost its header row and page 3 has no source anchor
The invoice total does not equal subtotal plus tax
Every field is present but the evidence is too thin to authorize a payment

variants.hint: Ask how many values you need to look at before the failure is visible.
variants.explanation: Each level needs a different amount of context, so a pipeline that only validates types will publish records that reconcile with nothing.

variants.title: Place the check at its level
variants.context: Validation happens at five levels: syntactic checks types and enumerations, field checks domain rules, structural checks sections, tables, and source anchors, cross-field checks reconciliation across values, and action validation asks whether the evidence is sufficient for the specific downstream decision.
variants.prompt: A second batch raises five more failures. Match each to its validation level.

pairs.label: A date field arrives as a string where the schema declares a date type
An account identifier fails its checksum rule
A multi-page table lost its continuation link between pages 4 and 5
The start date on page 1 falls after the end date on page 6
The record is complete but identity verification needs more than a blurred phone photo

variants.hint: One of these is a complete, valid record that still must not proceed.
variants.explanation: Action validation is the level that knows the consequence, which is why one confidence threshold cannot serve indexing and identity verification alike.

variants.title: Assign the intake disposition
variants.context: An intake record distinguishes four outcomes: accepted for parsing, unsupported when the file is valid but no approved route can process it, quarantined when corruption or suspicious expansion makes inspection unsafe, and rejected by policy when a product limit or authorization rule is violated.
variants.prompt: A tenant uploads a valid, uncorrupted CAD drawing. It passes every safety check, but no approved route in the product can parse that format. What disposition applies?
options: Record it as unsupported, because no approved route can process it.
Reject it by policy, because it violates the tenant's format authorization.
Quarantine it, because an unparsable file should be treated as unsafe.
optionFeedback: Unsupported is the outcome for a valid file that no approved route can handle, and it keeps the gap measurable.
No product limit or authorization rule was broken here, so a policy rejection would misreport the reason.
Quarantine is for corruption, malware, or suspicious expansion, and none of those apply to a clean file.
variants.hint: Ask whether the problem is with the file or with the routes available.
variants.explanation: The four intake outcomes carry different reasons and different follow-ups, so an unsupported format must not be logged as a safety event.

variants.title: Assign the intake disposition
variants.context: An intake record distinguishes four outcomes: accepted for parsing, unsupported when the file is valid but no approved route can process it, quarantined when corruption or suspicious expansion makes inspection unsafe, and rejected by policy when a product limit or authorization rule is violated.
variants.prompt: An uploaded archive is well formed but expands to 400 times its compressed size, far past the decompression budget. What disposition applies?
options: Quarantine it, because suspicious expansion makes inspection unsafe.
Record it as unsupported, because archives have no approved parsing route.
Raise the decompression budget for this tenant and retry the upload.
optionFeedback: Suspicious expansion is a named quarantine reason, and quarantine storage keeps it isolated from parsing.
The route exists and the archive is well formed, so the failure is a safety budget rather than a missing route.
Raising a budget to admit the file that tripped it removes the control that just worked.
variants.hint: Ask what the budget was protecting against when it tripped.
variants.explanation: Budgets are enforced before fan-out precisely so a decompression bomb is quarantined rather than expanded inside a parser.

variants.title: Assign the intake disposition
variants.context: An intake record distinguishes four outcomes: accepted for parsing, unsupported when the file is valid but no approved route can process it, quarantined when corruption or suspicious expansion makes inspection unsafe, and rejected by policy when a product limit or authorization rule is violated.
variants.prompt: A tenant on a 200-page plan limit uploads a clean, parseable 900-page bundle. What disposition applies?
options: Accept it for parsing and truncate the bundle at the 200th page.
Reject it by policy, because it exceeds a stated product limit.
Quarantine it, because an oversized bundle may be an abuse attempt.
optionFeedback: Silent truncation publishes an incomplete record while reporting success, which hides the limit from the tenant.
A stated product limit produces a policy rejection with a reason the tenant can act on.
Nothing about the file is corrupt or suspicious, so quarantine would mislabel a plan limit as a safety event.
variants.hint: Ask which of the four reasons a tenant could actually act on here.
variants.explanation: Policy rejection names a product rule rather than a defect, which keeps limit violations separate from safety and coverage problems.
